rows.name: Every market above, added together

source: The Federal Reserve's Financial Accounts for the United States (public corporate equities less exchange-traded and closed-end fund shares), OECD financial balance sheets (listed shares issued by residents, F511) for the other OECD economies, the Bank of Japan Flow of Funds, India's exchange shareholding filings and Taiwan's central bank Flow of Funds for the markets counted by the issuer's residence; the World Bank's World Development Indicators (market capitalisation of listed domestic companies, CM.MKT.LCAP.CD, CC BY 4.0) for the markets counted by exchange; converted with the International Monetary Fund's end-of-period exchange rates.
note: Each line is one economy's listed companies at market value, so adding the lines gives the world's listed equity without counting a company twice across lines. Two kinds of figure sit side by side and each line says which it is. Where a country's national accounts publish it, a company counts where it is registered, every quarter; that covers the United States, the euro-area countries, the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, India, Taiwan and the other OECD economies. Everywhere else the figure is the World Bank's compilation of the exchanges' own year-end totals, where a company counts where it is listed, so Hong Kong's line includes the mainland companies listed there. The United States is taken from the Federal Reserve's accounts with the shares of exchange-traded and closed-end funds taken out, because the Fed counts those fund units as company shares; the result is within about one per cent of the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq figures. India is taken from its exchange filings and never from the World Bank, whose Indian figure counts both of India's exchanges and reads about double. A yearly figure is carried forward for up to six quarters while the next year-end is awaited, a quarterly one for up to a year, and a market whose newest figure is older than that drops out rather than repeating a stale number. These markets are not added to the world ledger's total, because that ledger counts only the pools whose owners it can name; this chart is the denominator that ledger lacks for equity. Technical detail: OECD and national amounts are converted at the International Monetary Fund's end-of-period rate for the quarter, euro amounts only from 1999, any rate more than a year old refused; the World Bank's dollar amounts are used as published.
